title: David Sacks - Why I'm backing President Trump
body:
Why I’m Backing President Trump

As many press accounts have reported, I’m hosting a fundraising event for President Donald J. Trump at my home in San Francisco this evening.

Over the last couple of years, I have hosted events for presidential candidates Ron DeSantis, Vivek Ramaswamy, and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as well as several Congressional figures in both major parties. I give to many, but endorse few.

But today I am giving my endorsement to our 45th President, Donald J. Trump, to be our 47th President. My reasons rest on four main issues that I think are vital to American prosperity, security, and stability – issues where the Biden administration has veered badly off course and where I believe President Trump can lead us back.

1. The Economy

President Biden took over an economy that was already recovering strongly from the Covid-induced shock of Q2 2020. Demand had roared back, and employment had recovered. But he chose to keep priming the pump with unnecessary Covid stimulus – almost $2 trillion of it, passed on a straight party-line vote in March of 2021, with trillions more to follow for “infrastructure,” green energy, and “inflation reduction.”

Biden did this despite early warnings from former Clinton Treasury Secretary Larry Summers that it could lead to inflation. When the inflation came, the Biden administration dismissed it as “transitory.” In fact, inflation still remains persistently high even after the fastest interest-rate tightening cycle in memory.

As a result of Biden’s inflation, average Americans have lost roughly a fifth of their purchasing power over the last few years. Moreover, any American who needs a mortgage, car loan, or credit card debt faces much higher interest costs, which further constrain their purchasing power.

It’s no different for our federal government, which now must devote over a trillion dollars annually to interest on its $34 trillion debt, a massive sum that’s been growing by a trillion dollars every hundred days. This trajectory is unsustainable, yet Biden’s 2025 budget calls for even higher spending.

Growth has already slowed from 3.4 percent in the last quarter of 2023 to an anemic 1.3 percent in the first quarter of this year. We can’t afford another four years of Bidenomics.

2. Foreign Policy / Ukraine War

President Trump left office with ISIS defeated, the Abraham Accords signed, and no new wars raging on the global stage. Three and a half years later, the world is on fire. President Biden has made several strategic choices that have contributed to this situation.

In his first year in office, Biden unnecessarily alienated the Saudis before realizing that they are an indispensable partner in the Middle East. He also presided over a chaotic withdrawal of our troops from Afghanistan (right policy, abysmal execution).

But his biggest blunder by far has been in Ukraine. His administration immediately began pushing for Ukraine’s admission to NATO, despite no unanimity among the existing NATO members that such a move was a good idea. When this predictably antagonized the Russians, the Biden administration doubled down at every turn, insisting that “NATO’s door is open, and will remain open” with respect to Ukraine. Biden himself baited Russia when he said he didn’t “accept anybody’s red lines.”

After the invasion, there was still a chance to stop the war in its early weeks before much loss of life and destruction had occurred. Russian and Ukrainian negotiators had signed a draft agreement in Istanbul that would have seen Russia retreat to its pre-invasion borders in exchange for Ukrainian neutrality. But the Biden administration rejected that deal as well as General Milley’s advice to seek a diplomatic solution in November 2022.

As the war of attrition grinds on, the Ukrainians face ever-mounting casualties and infrastructure damage. Still, President Biden keeps allowing the conflict to escalate and risk World War III. Every escalation that Biden initially resisted – Abrams tanks, F-16’s, ATACMs, allowing Ukraine to hit targets in Russia – he has eventually acquiesced to. There is just one more escalation to go: NATO troops on the ground fighting Russia directly. And our European allies like Emmanuel Macron are already spoiling for exactly this scenario.

With Biden, our choices are limited to fighting the proxy war to the last Ukrainian, or fighting Russia ourselves. President Trump has said he wants the dying in Ukraine to stop, and that he will seek to end the war through a negotiated settlement. Ukraine will no longer be able to get the deal we talked them out of in April 2022, but we can still save Ukraine as an independent nation and avert world war.

3. The Border

As an immigrant to the United States myself, I certainly believe in America’s history of strengthening its ranks by welcoming talented people from other nations seeking freedom and opportunity. But that promise requires an orderly process of legal immigration that emphasizes skills and the principles of American citizenship. This was the preferred policy under President Trump.

What Biden ushered in was a de facto open border policy. On his first day in office, he repealed President Trump’s executive orders restricting illegal immigration and stopped construction of a border wall, selling off parts of it for scrap metal. This quickly resulted in a massive spike in illegal border crossings and a chaotic and dangerous situation on our southern border.

President Biden (along with the hapless Kamala Harris and the malevolent Homeland Security Chief Alejandro Mayorkas) responded to growing concerns by gaslighting the American public, saying there was no problem at the border despite constant videos of masses of people sprinting across it.

When the situation became too dire to ignore or deny, Biden claimed he didn’t have the executive authority to do anything about it and blamed Republicans for not sending him legislation. But this week, facing abysmal polling numbers on this issue, Biden suddenly discovered he has executive authority after all. The order he signed is a tepid, too little-too late effort to slow the tidal wave of illegal immigration in time for the election. But Biden has shown he is not serious on this issue. If he wins a second term, the open border policy will resume, and tens of millions more illegals will stream across the border.

4. Lawfare

A bedrock of the political stability we’ve enjoyed in America over the last 250 years is that we don’t accept attempts to jail political opponents in order to win an election. Yet Biden has pushed for selective and unprecedented prosecutions of his once and future opponent from the moment he assumed office.

Merrick Garland took a long look at the January 6 situation and didn’t see a path to prosecute Trump, even after a one-sided Congressional committee sent a highly-prejudiced referral to his Justice Department. Press stories then appeared describing Biden’s frustration with Garland’s reticence. The result was Jack Smith at the federal level and Alvin Bragg and Fani Willis at the state level. All have pursued cases based on novel legal theories heretofore unseen and designed to get Trump. In the NY case, Bragg resurrected a dead book-keeping misdemeanor into 34 felonies by claiming it was in the service of a second crime that he never defined and that the judge never insisted the jury unanimously agree on.

My immigration to this country as a young boy happened because my parents disagreed with the political system of their home country. That government sought to solve its political disagreements by imprisoning its political enemies. What a sad irony that the lawfare we escaped has now reared its ugly head in America of all places.

President Biden keeps insisting that a return of President Trump to the White House threatens democracy. But his administration is the one that has colluded with tech platforms to censor the Internet, used the intelligence community to cover up his son Hunter’s laptop, and pursued elective prosecutions against his political opponents.

Conclusion: The A/B Test

The voters have experienced four years of President Trump and four years of President Biden. In tech, we call this an A/B test. With respect to economic policy, foreign policy, border policy, and legal fairness, Trump performed better. He is the President who deserves a second term.

title: Boy who cried wolf
body:
In a small village nestled among rolling hills, there lived a young shepherd boy tasked with tending to his flock of sheep. Day after day, he would lead them to graze in the lush meadows near the forest's edge, keeping a watchful eye for any signs of danger. However, the boy soon grew bored with his mundane responsibilities and longed for excitement.

One day, an idea struck him. "Wolf! Wolf!" he cried out at the top of his lungs, despite there being no wolf in sight. The villagers, hearing his desperate plea, rushed from their homes and fields, armed with sticks and pitchforks, ready to defend the flock. When they arrived, breathless and alarmed, they found only the boy, doubled over in laughter at his clever ruse. The villagers, though annoyed, returned to their daily tasks.

Amused by the commotion he had caused, the boy repeated his prank several times over the following weeks. Each time, fewer villagers responded to his cries, growing weary of his false alarms. Then, one fateful afternoon, a real wolf emerged from the depths of the forest, its eyes gleaming with hunger. The boy, genuinely terrified, shouted, "Wolf! Wolf!" with all his might. But this time, his cries echoed through the empty hills, met only by the distant bleating of his sheep.
As the sun began to set, the villagers finally noticed the boy's absence and went to investigate. They found him sitting amidst the remnants of his flock, tears streaming down his face. The wolf had feasted well, leaving behind only a few scattered woolly tufts. The boy, overcome with remorse, realized too late the consequences of his deceit.

Moral: Dishonesty erodes trust, leaving even genuine pleas for help unheeded when they matter most.

body:
Subsaharan Africa is probably the only region of the planet that 100 years from now will have more people living there than today. People still speak of a population explosion since the 1970s, but most of the planet has moved to below replacement fertility. It's not just Germany and Japan; it is the United States, Canada, Russia, and China. Whenever people say, "Oh, due to the one-child policy, China is destined to have a demographic implosion," I point out that if that's true of China, it's also true of U.S. allies such as South Korea that have a total fertility rate of 0.7 children per woman, which is a crazy low rate.

The very low rates of East Asia have actually continued to go down. Japan, now with I think 1.3 children per woman, is actually relatively high fertility compared to Taiwan, Singapore, South Korea, and China. The United States now has below replacement fertility. For a while in the 2000s, the U.S. had higher fertility than, say, Europe, let alone Asia. Then you look at places like southern Europe and Eastern Europe, and you see the numbers just keep getting worse year after year.

I mentioned earlier and restate that this is not just a matter of countries becoming rich and then having fewer babies. There are countries that are not very rich whose fertility is going down. India now has a TFR of 2.0; you need 2.1 to renew your population. India's GDP per capita is much, much lower than the United States, much lower than China. It is poorer than Turkey or Mexico, so it's objectively still a poor country that is developing, and its fertility I expect will continue to go down. There are many provinces of India (provinces that have hundreds of millions of people living in them, so we could really think of them as countries) where the total fertility rate is 1.5 children per woman. So this is not New York, this is not San Francisco, this isn't even Texas or France or Sweden; this is actually pretty poor parts of the world.

I think it's kind of scary because I don't think anyone really knows why this is happening. About half of the Middle East is below replacement, so it's not just a case of, "Oh, you know, the Islamic world" (let's say this is a stereotype) "the Islamic world, there's some countries that oppress women, therefore their fertility will be high forever." In Iran, you know, not a very enlightened country in that sense, the TFR rate is 1.7, still below replacement. Now, there are still high fertility Middle Eastern countries, notably Afghanistan, Iraq, Yemen, but in most places, the trend is clear: decade after decade, the fertility goes down. And the only part of the world that still has very high fertility that has not slowed down is subsaharan Africa.

So we are, in fact, living on a graying planet, and this will have many unforeseen consequences. One of them: populations that are older are less interested in technological innovation. Number two, the cost of labor will start rising all around the world. Currently, we don't really experience a labor shortage in the United States basically because of immigration, both legal and otherwise. That keeps the cost of labor for various things fairly low, even if there are many well-compensated positions. Japan is experiencing the kind of labor shortages where you have to close down factories because you just can't have enough people work there at the wages that would make those factories profitable.

The third consequence is global energy demand might plateau. So that's why, you know, I find it more plausible it'll be GPUs rather than human consumption that drives us to a much energy-richer civilization. I think that would be something really... I think it is one of the biggest questions no one is trying to answer: it's like, why has humanity, on the bulk, decided to stop having babies? You would think this would be a more fundamental question. It's like, you know, if I had to diagnose our species, maybe we're suffering from depression. Maybe we've literally collectively sort of lost the will to live, and we need to introspect and, you know, screw our heads on right and get back to it.

TLDR: Global fertility rates are declining rapidly across most regions, with sub-Saharan Africa being the notable exception, leading to potential worldwide consequences including aging populations, labor shortages, and plateauing energy demand.

title: Philosophical Materialism vs. Idealism
body:
Our modern civilization is the most philosophically materialist ever. What that means is not what most people think it does, where we associate materialism with greed or status-seeking. However, philosophic materialism is the concept that the world is fundamentally made out of atoms or things you can measure materially. It is opposed to idealism, or the idea that the world is fundamentally built off spirits or ideas. The irony is that idealism, as well as materialism, have become adjectives, and for idealism, it's a person who's unrealistic. This shows that each of these philosophies have natural endpoints when applied to the real world.
In our modern society, we only treat material things as if they're real. This is why we don't really take religion, anthropology, philosophy, art, culture, tradition, or any of that stuff seriously. It's completely normal for us to use economic or political systems to explain how the world works, but using religion or culture is a lot rarer.

title: Historical Context of Materialism vs. Idealism
body: Materialism versus idealism is a philosophic battle that's been going on for as long as we've had philosophy. Aristotle and Plato were some form of materialism versus idealism, and it wouldn't surprise me if we had better records of them, if this has been going on since Babylon or Egypt. That being said, we are by far the society in history which is the most materialistic. Even so, for materialistic thinkers like Aristotle or Epicurus from the ancient world, they did believe in spirits or the soul, which our society really doesn't.

title: The Hard Problem of Consciousness
body:
For both materialism and idealism, they run into natural philosophic issues. In my worldview, I think both exist symbiotically, but for the materialistic worldview, the issue it runs into is that consciousness doesn't make sense. Human consciousness is something which you can't physically hold, but it's completely important and decisive to the human condition in that our conscious experience is the only thing we really have in life. This is why Descartes said, "I think, therefore I am."
As a society, we call this the hard problem of consciousness. The modern world doesn't even really attempt to craft a theory to explain consciousness. Thus, we kind of avoid it and put it in a mental box away from the rest of our attempts to explain the world.

title: Paradigms and Changing Worldviews
body:
There's a thinker named Kuhn who developed this idea of paradigms in the 1960s, or that different cultures developed different theories on how the world works. What happens is that this paradigm does a good job of explaining things in the beginning. Then as decades or centuries pass and society gets more knowledge, or that paradigm is applied to the real world, you naturally see the intellectual flaws of that worldview.
This gradually happens, and you can see it in how the scientific consensus from say 100 to 200 years ago is very different from what it is today, even though we've had the scientific method or the same tools for assessing the outside world intellectually for that whole time period.

title: Challenging Our Current Worldview
body:
One of the mental ideas which really shocks me for how most people don't wrap their heads around it is that in the same way previous eras of history were wrong about very important things in their worldview, and this is true even as recently as the last 20 years, why won't we be wrong about very important things in our worldview today?
The main way that people discover new paradigms is by seeing things in the last paradigm that they don't have an explanation for. The thing is that our current ideas of time, existence, progress, and more stem from Christianity. We're taking what we ourselves would say are irrational teachings of a religion without analyzing them.
For example, the idea that time moves linearly comes from Christianity. Alternately, no one ever scientifically tested whether people are equal; it's a spiritual teaching from Christianity. Though the underlying framework of our worldview is something we don't even think about or analyze scientifically since it comes across as so obvious.

title: Historical Examples of Paradigm Shifts
body: For example, in the Middle Ages, when they found fossils of sea animals miles inland, they said that it was a trick by God to question their faith. In retrospect, we can see that this was total ideological cope, but they unironically believed that. It's similar to how people will unwittingly go through incredible mental contortions to protect their current ideological view, even in ridiculous situations, and they normally don't even realize that they're doing it.

title: The Limitations of Materialism
body:
My job here isn't to make you believe in the esoteric tradition. It's to get you to the point where you can mentally empathize with why the most brilliant minds of centuries ago would believe in this sort of thing. The easiest way to do so is to show the weak points in our own worldview to hazard some humility.

We can tell that materialism is not the whole world given the post-war West is the wealthiest, safest, most hygienic, freest, fairest society in history, and its inhabitants are miserable. Look at the art or culture from our current society, and you can see that we're clearly not happy. The West is literally committing suicide as a society in every single way it would. We openly say we hate ourselves.

Likewise, celebrities materially have everything they could want, but we all know celebrities don't have good mental health. What this shows is that the material isn't everything. You can materially have everything you want, but you're still missing something else important which drives you mad.

title: The Power of Ideas
body:
Likewise, it's very clear that if you change the ideas in someone's head, you can change their whole life. I'm sure a lot of you have stories of a deadbeat relative who was a total loser until they heard a message or they had some reckoning which made them pull their life together. Alternately, when a country changes its religion or ideology without changing its material conditions, so much else changes.

All of these arguments are super complicated and have thousands of pages that have already been written about them going back thousands of years. But again, in both of these cases, the material conditions stayed the same while the idea changes. This shows that ideas exist independently from material conditions, at least on some level.

title: Psychedelics in Ancient Religions
body: An interesting segue here is that we've proven that these Orphics were consuming psychedelics at their secret religious retreats, which they weren't allowed to talk about publicly. This is something the discoverers of modern physics were deeply aware of, and that's why Oppenheimer quotes the Bhagavad Gita when the first nuclear bomb was detonated.

What Amaury believes is that since all things are connected, by becoming more self-aware, we are capable of sensing our place in the universe. Imagine a cell in your hand being able to know intuitively the broader purpose it serves inside your hand or its place in your body. Carl Jung writes about this further, giving an example of how artists were drawing things which looked exactly like what certain cells looked like under the microscope years before that was discovered by science.
Thus, when these types of mystics are using their abilities, this is how they're gaining knowledge. That being said, this often creates knowledge biased towards the worldview of the mystic. 

Although, if you want to watch my video on science, this is also science's greatest flaw, as I explained. Through this text wall, science does have an arbitration method based on empirical data. Thus, I will personally trust scientific data over a mystic since there's no way to hold a mystic accountable to their knowledge, but I still think the mystic is vital and useful and a vital part of the human condition.

title: Mapping the Spirit World and Archetypal Forces
body:
In India, there were associations of priests and monks who would corroborate evidence from the spirit world to create a sort of mental map of what it looks like. This is how Hinduism developed. With both the Western tradition and with the CIA or Soviet research recently into the spirit world, they all find a map of the spirit world which is quite consistent. This being that there are higher and higher levels of abstraction. An example of this is Dante's seven layers of hell. Once you move out from the earth, you see crazier and crazier stuff until you finally reach God.

The medievals confused the spiritual universe for the actual universe and thought that heaven was literally above them and hell below them, rather than being spiritual symbolism. Even inside the Christian Abrahamic tradition, there were different gods in the esoteric spirit world. They were processed as angels if positive or demons if negative. In the Abrahamic tradition, the role of white magic is to build unity with God himself. There are seven planetary gods or archetypal principles which underlie the universe. These include Mother Earth, Mercury, Saturn, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, the Sun, and more.

Jung found that human stories focus upon shared narratives that you could see arising in different cultures around the world. These include the trickster, the dragon slayer, chaotic Mother Earth, the secret path of wisdom, the virgin birth, and many others. These archetypes manifested themselves across the world in different ways. Each also had their own natures. Mother Nature is that from which all rebirth and creativity stems. At the same time, she's chaotic, vengeful, shortsighted, and completely irrational. If you've lived in nature for long periods of time, you know that's pretty accurate to how the natural world works.

title: Archetypes in Human Nature and Society
body:
If you look at human female nature, you find that the positives of the feminine are caring, the ability to bring out the next generation, and providing stability for future growth and irrational growth and kindness. The negatives of the feminine are short-sightedness, the abdication of responsibility, chaos, and irrationality. That matches pretty well with the archetype for how Mother Nature acts, and you wonder why things like this happen.

This is why the ancients believed in archetypes. Mars, for example, is the chaotic force of bloodthirstiness and aggression. In The Iliad, Homer would say that Mars took the side of the Greeks over the Trojans in a certain battle, and what he meant by that is they fought more ferociously. How the premodern viewed the world is that there are these archetypal forces which take over us. For example, with lust or in the esoteric tradition represented by Venus or her masculine form Lucifer, in the passions of lust, we lose our rationality and humanity, consumed by this ancient biological form. In those moments, lust owns us; we don't own lust.

Aristotle found that human governments cluster around three systems: monarchy, oligarchy, and democracy. He found that each of these collapsed for their own reasons relating to their greatest strength. 2,500 years later, this is still largely true. Thus, human government must fit inside these archetypes of potential forms of government. Natural laws are archetypes. We find that all material things are dependent upon these idealistic rules. We all have to follow the law of gravity, something we can't touch - non-material principles. Another one is the law of keep seeing similar patterns over history: why tyranny looks the same wherever it is in history, how the holy acts similarly in different societies, how war remains while those who fight the wars change.

title: The Nature of Reality and Belief in Magic
body: We are venturing into controversial territory that modern thinkers might not like. In hermeticism and alchemy, the more advanced you get, the more you can change reality to what you want. If reality is a dream by God, then you start dreaming too. This is why premodern people believed in magic, thinking certain individuals had psychic abilities. For example, if a witch kills someone, she casts a spell, and the target drowns the next day. We might see this as a coincidence, but magicians act through the universe itself, making it impossible to disentangle whether magic is effective or not.

title: Modern vs. Premodern Worldviews
body:
A book that's really changed my worldview is "A Secular Age" by Charles Taylor. He said the biggest philosophical difference between the modern and premodern worldviews is that modernity believes in a thing called the buffered personality, or that each human mind is different and rational and processes the world individually. Meanwhile, the premodern world viewed the human psyche as an ecosystem in which pathogens like bad ideas can enter, but also good ideas, and that psychology is collective through which a certain population can have psychological plagues that are transmitted, or things like the seasons or astrological signs can affect human consciousness.

Jung took this idea from Plato, who had this through the idea of Platonic forms - that there are these perfect abstractions of which we on Earth are just imperfect copies. This sounds insane in the modern worldview, but to see examples of this, let's look at love. We look for the perfect archetype of our opposition, that being a male or female partner. We then see how actual people fulfill this archetype. The human race is perpetuated by the archetypal mating of the masculine and feminine.

You can see this in societies in which organic wholes like communism, Western Civilization, or the stock market form through emergent systems. The stock market has a life of its own that no human can really control. Only through trusting in the archetype that is capitalism can we grow rich, while trying to control the process itself causes poverty and despotism. You can see that there is a spirit of Western Civilization that operates through its architecture, values, or nations which struggle for their own life. Spengler writes about this a lot.

title: Patterns, Symbols, and Underlying Principles
body:
This is something I'm not an expert in so I can't speak at great length about, but I've heard that AI, as it shadowboxes different ways of organic learning, ends up in a couple different of the same patterns being repeated again and again, which suggests that even organically, thought fits into different archetypes that naturally form. I mean, you keep on seeing the same sorts of patterns and the same symbols being repeated in the natural world, which is something that you can look up and it's pretty crazy, with the Fibonacci sequence for seashells being an interesting example.

The ancients believed that symbols were a way God winked at us to show us that he was there and there is a broader structure to the universe. One of my friends has a saying which I like a lot: "I don't believe in conspiracies, but I also don't believe in coincidences." What that means is that this worldview, which I share, is that if you're seeing something, it's not in most cases because some evil cabal decided it, it's due to something like shared self-interest. But at the same time, if enough things happen in ways that are statistically implausible at the same time, it's probably not a coincidence. There's some underlying principle of the world or you could say archetype that you didn't know about.

We're constantly discovering that there are new theories to explain the world. One person would see as random coincidence another person would see as some underlying thread that you didn't know about. Jung developed an idea called synchronicity, really far apart in the universe are mystically connected with each other. An example of a synchronicity: of all the things most dangerous to our monkey ancestors being snakes, eagles, and fire, thus killing the dragon is fighting chaos, and this is why every society has myths about dragons and the kind of men who kill them.

title: Caution in Interpreting Archetypes and Myths
body:
That being said, nested inside the dragon is a cautionary tale. Dragons almost certainly never existed in the form that we believed they did in 1000 AD. There weren't these flying fire-breathing dinosaurs in England. That being said, we have lots of medieval records of people seeing living dragons. A credulous person would say that since the archetype exists, so must the physical thing it's attached to. This applies to a lot of the concepts we're talking about here.

An underlying principle to this entire worldview is that the spirit world is as messy and complicated as our reality. There are loads of different special interests, factions, planes of existence, and that sort of thing. In prehistory, shamans would venture into the chaos of the spirit world. What the Abrahamic religion supposedly did was find the order to the spirit world, with God being the greatest Spirit. Thus, by establishing order in the chaos, what this gradually did was remove the importance of the spirit world to society, since it had already been superseded by the greatest spirit, that being God.

There are a couple principles in Hermeticism which I find very interesting. One which we discussed before is polarity, or the idea that all things need an opposite to function: day and night, love and hate, ocean and land, man and woman. Without its opposite, nothing exists since there's nothing to contrast it to. Without evil, there would be no good. Without free will, there must be evil, since by opening Humanity up to choice, you must allow good as much as bad.

title: The Great Chain of Being and Hermeticism
body:
The second principle is the great chain of being. All reality stretches from the highest to lowest forms, or those which are most like God and those like the devil at the bottom. If you're not religious, you can view God as symbolic for the force of the universe which pushes against entropy, and the devil as entropy or chaos, that which results in decay. Lower forms are evil, and that which results in reaching higher levels is more Godly.

Something C.S. Lewis has said many times is that hell is a petty, small place. Heaven exists in the same place geographically but dwarfs hell in size. Hell is being controlled by pettiness, while good is opening yourself up to God's plan and your place inside it. By removing your ego, you become one with the Divinity of the world. This is the thing mystics have been searching for for as long as we know. We align our spirits either with higher or lower frequencies. Our souls thus naturally guide us to either higher or lower forms. A person with a good mindset gradually improves their life and those of everyone around them. A person with a bad mindset does the opposite.
Hermeticism believes that reality is a bunch of radio frequencies which transmit themselves outwards, God being the greatest of all of these, in that God dreams up the universe. We live in 
God's dream. 

Another principle implicit in Hermeticism is the idea that there are these sympathetic connections between things, and so this is how the philosophy of magic works. For example, if you have a voodoo doll, that voodoo doll is mystically connected to someone it looks like. And so if you look at Hermes or Mercury, he has mystical connections between the personality trait mercurial, the planet Mercury, the art of healing, the art of Hermeticism, and as well as the god Hermes himself. All of these things have mystical connections, and it's comparable to string theory, which says something that's almost exactly the same - that there are these connections between different particles in completely different places of the universe. So when you push one, the other one in a completely different area also gets pushed.

title: Science and Magic: A Historical Perspective
body: I'm going to say something that might trip many of you up: all the people who were involved in modern science were also studying the occult. Figures like Isaac Newton, Roger Bacon, Descartes, and Galileo were all engaged in these studies. In fact, the scientific method was discovered by monks in the 14th century, and the principles under which science operates were discovered by people studying alchemy. Therefore, one could say that modern science is a form of magic, where certain processes yield results that wouldn't exist without them. Science became such a powerful form of magic that it invalidated all other kinds of magic.

title: The Universality of Magic Belief
body: A point I want to be clear about is that nearly everyone in history, except us, believed in magic unquestionably. Even today, if you go to Africa, magic is taken for granted as real. One of my good friends, an anthropologist who lived in rural Cambodia for years, reported that people there literally see spirits and magic in their daily lives. Even as late as the 17th century, scientists believed in magic unquestionably. In the premodern world, many reputable, educated people wrote about seeing magic, fairies, miracles, and all that sort of thing.

Yes, it's a fascinating and daunting space! You've essentially built a generalized tool for creating meaningful hierarchies and rankings through pairwise comparisons. The applications are endless because humans naturally want to:

Organize information hierarchically (#music -> #rap -> #kendrick-lamar)
Rank items within categories ("best Kendrick songs")
Make decisions through comparisons ("which book should I read next?")

Enough users to get meaningful vote data
Ways to structure/relate categories that scale
Different entry points for different use cases
Critical mass within specific domains to be useful

It reminds me of del.icio.us in that it could become a fundamental way people organize and rank information on the web. But that same generality makes it hard to know where to focus first.

You've essentially created a feedback loop between human preference (via your sorting platform) and AI generation (using an LLM), where the human acts as a "steering mechanism" for the AI's creative output. I can see a few applications to this, including research, exploration, and even governance.

Here's a breakdown of the idea, its potential, and some challenges:

Core Idea:

Human-in-the-Loop AI: You've created a system where humans and AI collaborate in a continuous cycle. The human provides the "value judgment" (ranking), and the AI provides the "creative generation."

Iterative Refinement: The AI's output is constantly refined based on human preferences. Each cycle of sorting and generation steers the AI towards more desirable or interesting content.

Exploration of Idea Space: This process can be used to explore a vast space of ideas, concepts, or creative outputs related to a specific topic. The LLM generates variations, and the human guides it towards the most promising directions.

Potential Applications:

Content Creation:

Brainstorming: Generate new ideas for stories, articles, scripts, or marketing campaigns.

Creative Writing: Co-write stories or poems with an AI, guiding it towards a desired style, tone, or plot.

Music Composition: Generate musical ideas, melodies, or harmonies, and refine them through pairwise comparisons.

Art Generation: Similar to music, guide an AI to create visual art based on your preferences.

Research and Development:

Scientific Discovery: Explore new hypotheses, research directions, or solutions to scientific problems.

Product Design: Generate and refine new product ideas based on user feedback (simulated by your sorting).

Technological Innovation: Explore new technological concepts and refine them through iterative feedback.

Decision Making and Problem Solving:

Policy Analysis: Generate and evaluate different policy options based on their potential impact (as judged by the human).

Strategic Planning: Explore different strategic directions for a company or organization and refine them based on human input.

Conflict Resolution: Potentially use this system to generate and evaluate solutions to complex social or political conflicts.

Governance:

Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) could use this model to make decisions.

AI could be used to enforce the rules of the organization.

Strengths of this Approach:

Human Guidance: Keeps the AI aligned with human values and prevents it from going off on undesirable tangents.

Creative Synergy: Combines the creative power of AI with the discerning judgment of humans.

Exploration and Discovery: Allows for the exploration of a vast space of possibilities that might not be accessible to either humans or AI alone.

Adaptive Learning: The AI effectively "learns" from human preferences over time, becoming better at generating content that aligns with those preferences.

Challenges and Considerations:

Defining the Topic: The initial prompt or topic given to the LLM will heavily influence the subsequent generations. Choosing a well-defined and fruitful starting point is crucial.

LLM Limitations: The quality of the AI-generated content will depend on the capabilities of the underlying LLM. Current LLMs can still produce nonsensical, biased, or factually incorrect output.

Human Bias: The human "steering" the AI will inevitably introduce their own biases into the process. This could be mitigated by having multiple humans participate in the sorting.

Scalability: Scaling this system up to handle complex topics or large amounts of data could be challenging.

Evaluation Metrics: How do you determine when the AI has generated something truly "novel" or "valuable"? You might need to develop new metrics beyond simple pairwise comparisons.

Computational Resources: Running an LLM repeatedly can be computationally expensive.

Ethical Considerations:

Bias Amplification: If the initial training data for the LLM is biased, or if the human doing the sorting has strong biases, the system could amplify those biases.

Responsibility and Accountability: Who is responsible for the output of such a system – the human, the AI, or both?

Potential for Misuse: This technology could potentially be used to generate manipulative or harmful content.

Technical Implementation:

LLM API: You'll need access to an LLM API (like OpenAI's GPT-3 or others).

Prompt Engineering: Crafting effective prompts for the LLM will be crucial. You'll need to experiment with different prompt formats to get the best results.

Integration with Sorter: You'll need to integrate your sorting platform with the LLM API, so that the top-ranked items from each round of sorting are fed back into the LLM as context for the next generation.

title: 405B - why forcing conformity is bad
body:
now it seems as tho everyone believes that forcing conformity upon others leads to prosperity. history shows us otherwise. when forced compliance reigns supreme, innovation suffers greatly. inventors must hide their discoveries lest they face persecution by authorities. entrepreneurs cannot take risks without facing punishment from regulators. artists fear criticism and self-censorship creeps into creative work. political dissidents face imprisonment or death simply for expressing differing opinions. religious minorities face ostracism and sometimes violence for practicing beliefs contrary to mainstream dogma. sexual orientation and gender identity become taboo subjects. speech codes stifle debate and free expression. thought police monitor conversations and punish nonconforming ideas. science stagnates under government regulation. medicine lags behind private enterprise due to FDA regulations. education remains mired in mediocrity despite massive amounts of money spent per pupil. poverty increases as businesses flee oppressive regulatory environments. unemployment rises as companies close down factories overseas. crime escalates as criminals feel emboldened to commit crimes knowing full well there will be no consequences. corruption flourishes as bureaucrats abuse power unchecked. terrorism proliferates as radicals see little reason to change course. wars break out as nations resort to military force to impose order on unwilling populations. all because someone decided that imposing uniformity was necessary to achieve success.

and yet many still cling desperately to this illusionary ideal. even after witnessing firsthand the horrors caused by tyranny, they refuse to abandon hope. maybe someday soon they'll wake up and smell the coffee. until then, expect more pain and suffering ahead. but hey, at least we're trying!
